fields.label: Cards ×4
rows: 🛑 It has to live in oil

A filler cap sits in hot oil vapour for the life of the engine. NBR is the standard answer, AEM where the oil runs hotter than +120 °C. Weather compounds swell in oil and soften — we will say so rather than quote one.
Tight enough to seal, loose enough to remove

The cap seals on an interference fit against the neck bore, and it is taken off by hand with oily fingers. Too much interference and it gets levered off with a screwdriver — then it is damaged and it leaks. We set the fit and the grip together.
🛑 Sealed or vented is not a detail

A crankcase builds pressure, and some fillers need to breathe through the cap while others must not. Fit a sealed cap where a vented one belongs and the pressure leaves through the next weakest seal — tell us which you need.
The seal is the lip, and it takes a set

A sealing lip that flattens loses its interference and starts to weep. We test compression set in-house to ASTM D395 Method B and report it, because on this part it is the difference between a cap that seals at year one and one that seals at year five.
fields.note:
Four cards, four cards — no count change and no new element.
Card 03 names a failure mode most buyers have met and never traced. A gearbox or engine that pushes oil out of an unrelated seal is often a venting problem at the filler, and it is diagnosed almost nowhere.
Card 02 is the design tension in two sentences, and it explains why removal force belongs on the drawing

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.chip: The sealing lip and the vent belong in the process
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps · the same text as all 31 pages

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. The compound is chosen for oil resistance at the filler-neck temperature before anything else.

Mould design and CNC tool manufacture, in-house, held as a controlled record. The sealing lip and the head grip are cut together, since one sets how well the cap seals and the other whether it can be removed by hand.
Compression moulding, with the vent formed in the tool where a vented cap is specified.
Post-cure and deflashing. Flash on the sealing lip is a leak path, and flash across a vent closes it.
Quality inspection — sealing lip diameter gauged against the neck bore, plus hardness, dimensional check and compression set on batch samples.
Export packaging — industrial packing with documentation. Caps are bagged loose so the sealing lip is not deformed in transit. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber packaging is used.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept. The live text says “ISO-certified lab” in step 01, which becomes “in-house lab”; step 03 says “Compression Moulding” alone and gains the vent; step 04 is “Post-Cure & Trimming” and gains the two flash consequences.
Step 04 is worth the clause because it names two different failures — flash on a lip leaks, flash over a vent blocks it, and a blocked vent on a cap sold as vented is worse than no vent at all, because nobody looks for it.
Step 05 gauges the lip against the bore, which is the check that stops a batch arriving that seals on paper and weeps in service
